claim: RNA polymerase II (Pol II) pausing is a general regulatory step in transcription.
source: RNA polymerase II (Pol II) pausing is a general regulatory step in transcription, yet the stability of paused Pol II varies widely between genes.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: The stability of paused Pol II varies widely between genes.
source: RNA polymerase II (Pol II) pausing is a general regulatory step in transcription, yet the stability of paused Pol II varies widely between genes.
evidence: This statement is supported by experimental data and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: Paused Pol II stability correlates with core promoter elements.
source: Although paused Pol II stability correlates with core promoter elements, the contribution of individual sequences remains unclear, in part because no rapid assay is available for measuring the changes in Pol II pausing as a result of altered promoter sequences.
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated through genome-wide analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: ChIP-nexus captures endogenous Pol II pausing on transfected plasmids.
source: Here, we overcome this hurdle by showing that ChIP-nexus captures the endogenous Pol II pausing on transfected plasmids.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The pausing stability is influenced by downstream promoter sequences.
source: Using this reporter-ChIP-nexus assay in Drosophila cells, we show that the pausing stability is influenced by downstream promoter sequences, but that the strongest contribution to Pol II pausing comes from the initiator sequence, in which a single nucleotide, a G at the +2 position, is critical for stable Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from promoter swapping experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: The strongest contribution to Pol II pausing comes from the initiator sequence.
source: Using this reporter-ChIP-nexus assay in Drosophila cells, we show that the pausing stability is influenced by downstream promoter sequences, but that the strongest contribution to Pol II pausing comes from the initiator sequence, in which a single nucleotide, a G at the +2 position, is critical for stable Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: A G at the +2 position of the initiator sequence is critical for stable Pol II pausing.
source: Using this reporter-ChIP-nexus assay in Drosophila cells, we show that the pausing stability is influenced by downstream promoter sequences, but that the strongest contribution to Pol II pausing comes from the initiator sequence, in which a single nucleotide, a G at the +2 position, is critical for stable Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is supported by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: After initiating transcription at the transcription start site (TSS), Pol II often pauses 30–50 bp downstream of the TSS.
source: After initiating transcription at the transcription start site (TSS), Pol II often pauses 30–50 bp downstream of the TSS, before being released by p-TEFb into productive elongation (Adelman and Lis, 2012; Gaertner and Zeitlinger, 2014; Yamaguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Paused Pol II is released by p-TEFb into productive elongation.
source: After initiating transcription at the transcription start site (TSS), Pol II often pauses 30–50 bp downstream of the TSS, before being released by p-TEFb into productive elongation (Adelman and Lis, 2012; Gaertner and Zeitlinger, 2014; Yamaguchi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Genome-wide profiling of Pol II and nascent transcripts suggest that pausing is widespread across the genome.
source: Genome-wide profiling of Pol II and nascent transcripts suggest that pausing is widespread across the genome (Core et al., 2008; Muse et al., 2007; Nechaev et al., 2010; Zeitlinger et al., 2007), and inhibition of p-TEFb blocks the productive elongation of the majority of active genes (Chao and Price, 2001; Jonkers et al., 2014; Ni et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to genome-wide studies.

claim: Inhibition of p-TEFb blocks the productive elongation of the majority of active genes.
source: Genome-wide profiling of Pol II and nascent transcripts suggest that pausing is widespread across the genome (Core et al., 2008; Muse et al., 2007; Nechaev et al., 2010; Zeitlinger et al., 2007), and inhibition of p-TEFb blocks the productive elongation of the majority of active genes (Chao and Price, 2001; Jonkers et al., 2014; Ni et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Pause release is a general and obligatory step in transcription.
source: Together, these results suggest that pause release is a general and obligatory step in transcription.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited studies on p-TEFb inhibition and genome-wide pausing.

claim: The degree of pausing may be influenced by transcriptional activation.
source: While the degree of pausing may be influenced by transcriptional activation (Buckley et al., 2014; Danko et al., 2013; Min et al., 2011; Rahl et al., 2010), differences in Pol II pausing across the genome are, to a large extent, a property of the promoter.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Differences in Pol II pausing across the genome are, to a large extent, a property of the promoter.
source: While the degree of pausing may be influenced by transcriptional activation (Buckley et al., 2014; Danko et al., 2013; Min et al., 2011; Rahl et al., 2010), differences in Pol II pausing across the genome are, to a large extent, a property of the promoter.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data and citations in the manuscript.

claim: In the early Drosophila embryo, Pol II pausing is most frequently found at developmental control genes.
source: In the early Drosophila embryo, Pol II pausing is most frequently found at developmental control genes, and a large portion of these genes remain highly paused throughout embryonic development independently of their expression (Gaertner et al., 2012; Zeitlinger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A large portion of highly paused genes remain highly paused throughout embryonic development independently of their expression.
source: In the early Drosophila embryo, Pol II pausing is most frequently found at developmental control genes, and a large portion of these genes remain highly paused throughout embryonic development independently of their expression (Gaertner et al., 2012; Zeitlinger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The promoter sequences of highly paused genes are notably enriched for specific core promoter elements.
source: The promoter sequences of such highly paused genes are notably enriched for specific core promoter elements (Hendrix et al., 2008), and promoter swapping experiments demonstrate that Pol II pausing depends on the promoter sequence (Lagha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Promoter swapping experiments demonstrate that Pol II pausing depends on the promoter sequence.
source: The promoter sequences of such highly paused genes are notably enriched for specific core promoter elements (Hendrix et al., 2008), and promoter swapping experiments demonstrate that Pol II pausing depends on the promoter sequence (Lagha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: A large fraction of promoters in the Drosophila genome have clearly defined core promoter sequences that are associated with strong Pol II pausing.
source: Drosophila is ideally suited to study the relationship between promoter sequences and Pol II pausing since a large fraction of promoters in the Drosophila genome have clearly defined core promoter sequences that are associated with strong Pol II pausing (Chen et al., 2013; Gilchrist et al., 2010; Hendrix et al., 2008; Juven-Gershon and Kadonaga, 2010; Kwak et al., 2013; Lee et al., 1992; Vo Ngoc et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Highly paused promoters typically undergo focused initiation.
source: Moreover, these highly paused promoters typically undergo focused initiation, during which Pol II begins transcription at a defined genomic position within a window of a few nucleotides (Hoskins et al., 2011; Kwak et al., 2013; Ni et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Highly paused promoters do not typically show strong +1 nucleosomes near the pause site.
source: Finally, these highly paused promoters do not typically show strong +1 nucleosomes near the pause site, making Pol II pausing less likely to be dependent on chromatin context (Benjamin and Gilmour, 1998; Bondarenko et al., 2006; Brown et al., 1996; Gaertner et al., 2012; Gilchrist et al., 2010; Izban and Luse, 1991; Jimeno-González et al., 2015; Kwak et al., 2013; Rach et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The core promoter elements of highly paused promoters in Drosophila are recognized by the basal transcription factor TFIID.
source: Their core promoter elements are recognized by the basal transcription factor TFIID, a highly conserved multi-subunit complex whose promoter binding specificity appears to be conserved across metazoans.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations.

claim: TFIID is a highly conserved multi-subunit complex whose promoter binding specificity appears to be conserved across metazoans.
source: Their core promoter elements are recognized by the basal transcription factor TFIID, a highly conserved multi-subunit complex whose promoter binding specificity appears to be conserved across metazoans.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Recent cryo-EM structures of TFIID show human TFIID bound to all core promoter elements of the synthetic Drosophila super core promoter.
source: For example, recent cryo-EM structures of TFIID show human TFIID bound to all core promoter elements of the synthetic Drosophila super core promoter, including the sequences enriched among highly paused promoters (Louder et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: TFIID interacts with sequence elements at three regions along the core promoter.
source: TFIID interacts with sequence elements at three regions along the core promoter, which are spaced in a fixed distance from each other (Juven-Gershon and Kadonaga, 2010; Louder et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2018; Vo Ngoc et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TATA box is located ~30 bp upstream of the transcription start site.
source: The first contact occurs at the TATA box, a well-studied core promoter element that is located ~30 bp upstream of the transcription start site and is bound by TATA-binding protein (TBP), a component of TFIID (Chasman et al., 1993; Kim et al., 1993a; Kim et al., 1993b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TATA box is bound by TATA-binding protein (TBP), a component of TFIID.
source: The first contact occurs at the TATA box, a well-studied core promoter element that is located ~30 bp upstream of the transcription start site and is bound by TATA-binding protein (TBP), a component of TFIID (Chasman et al., 1993; Kim et al., 1993a; Kim et al., 1993b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and established knowledge.

claim: The initiator (Inr) sequence overlaps the nucleotide where Pol II initiates transcription.
source: The second contact occurs at the initiator (Inr) sequence, which overlaps the nucleotide where Pol II initiates transcription (referred to as the +1) (Chalkley and Verrijzer, 1999; Emami et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Inr is the most common core promoter element in metazoans.
source: The Inr is the most common core promoter element in metazoans and is often the only identifiable core promoter element in mammalian promoters (Hoskins et al., 2011; Ohler et al., 2002; Smale and Kadonaga, 2003; Vo Ngoc et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The third DNA region contacted by TFIID lies ~30 bp downstream of the transcription start site.
source: The third DNA region contacted by TFIID lies ~30 bp downstream of the transcription start site. It contains short sequence motifs such as the downstream promoter element (DPE), motif ten element (MTE), and the pause button (PB) (Burke and Kadonaga, 1996; Hendrix et al., 2008; Kutach and Kadonaga, 2000; Lim et al., 2004; Purnell et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Measurements of paused Pol II across the genome normally do not assess the duration of pausing directly, but rather represent steady-state Pol II occupancy across a population of cells.
source: Measurements of paused Pol II across the genome, including with ChIP-seq, normally do not assess the duration of pausing directly, but rather represent steady-state Pol II occupancy across a population of cells, in which paused Pol II turns over at different rates.
evidence: This is based on the understanding of ChIP-seq methodology.

claim: Triptolide inhibits initiation globally and prevents new Pol II from reaching the pause position.
source: Triptolide inhibits initiation globally and prevents new Pol II from reaching the pause position (Jonkers et al., 2014; Titov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: After triptolide treatment, previously existing paused Pol II is lost over time, either by transitioning into elongation or due to premature transcript termination.
source: After triptolide treatment, previously existing paused Pol II is lost over time, either by transitioning into elongation or due to premature transcript termination.
evidence: This is based on the mechanism of triptolide action and observations from cited studies.

claim: The decay rate of paused Pol II under triptolide treatment is proportional to the stability of paused Pol II.
source: The decay rate of paused Pol II under these conditions is then proportional to the stability of paused Pol II (Henriques et al., 2013; Jonkers et al., 2014; Krebs et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ChIP-nexus has the advantage of distinguishing Pol II signal at the site of initiation and pausing.
source: This assay has the advantage of distinguishing Pol II signal at the site of initiation and pausing, and thus the Pol II half-life calculations are based on paused Pol II, rather than total Pol II at the promoter (Shao and Zeitlinger, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: Time-course measurements of paused Pol II across the Drosophila melanogaster genome confirmed large differences in pausing stability across promoters.
source: These experiments confirmed the large differences in pausing stability across promoters and showed significant correlations with core promoter elements.
evidence: This is based on data from a previous study by the authors.

claim: Paused Pol II can easily be detected on a plasmid by ChIP-nexus.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that paused Pol II can easily be detected on a plasmid by ChIP-nexus and its footprint closely recapitulates the Pol II footprint at the endogenous locus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The Pol II footprint on a plasmid closely recapitulates the Pol II footprint at the endogenous locus.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that paused Pol II can easily be detected on a plasmid by ChIP-nexus and its footprint closely recapitulates the Pol II footprint at the endogenous locus.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The Inr sequence, when containing a G at position +2, plays an unexpectedly large and dominant role in stabilizing paused Pol II.
source: Using this novel assay, termed reporter-ChIP-nexus, we analyzed the contribution of various core promoter elements and discovered that the Inr sequence, when containing a G at position +2, plays an unexpectedly large and dominant role in stabilizing paused Pol II.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Strong Pol II pausing was observed at the synthetic super core promoter (SCP).
source: Results of reporter-ChIP-nexus reveal strong Pol II pausing at the synthetic super core promoter (SCP), which contains the core promoter elements TATA, Inr, MTE, DPE and PB (top).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with ChIP-nexus data.

claim: The vast majority of RNAs from the SCP promoter start at the expected site of initiation.
source: The results for the SCP promoter show that the vast majority of RNAs start at the expected site of initiation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with 5' RNA sequencing data.

claim: D. pseudoobscura promoters are sufficiently different from those in the melanogaster genome to facilitate unambiguous mapping of Pol II signal on the plasmid.
source: D. pseudoobscura promoters are sufficiently different from those in the melanogaster genome (due to ~25 millions of years of divergence), thereby facilitating the unambiguous mapping of Pol II signal on the plasmid.
evidence: This is based on evolutionary divergence and is used as a rationale for the experimental design.

claim: The start sites on all plasmids mapped within a narrow window of a few base pairs to the predicted Inr sequence.
source: On all plasmids, the start sites mapped within a narrow window of a few base pairs to the predicted Inr sequence (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by 5' RNA sequencing data in Figure 2A.

claim: The Pol II profile on each plasmid was in most cases indistinguishable from the endogenous Pol II profile.
source: Moreover, the Pol II profile was in most cases indistinguishable from the endogenous Pol II profile (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), with Pearson correlations similar to or slightly below those of replicate experiments (Table S2 and S3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing ChIP-nexus data from plasmids and endogenous loci in Figure 2A.

claim: Lifting a promoter with TFIID-dependent core promoter elements out of its genomic chromatin context does not abolish Pol II pausing.
source: This indicates that lifting a promoter with TFIID-dependent core promoter elements out of its genomic chromatin context does not abolish Pol II pausing and confirms that the pausing profile at those promoters is highly dependent on the promoter sequence.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Pol II pausing is recapitulated on plasmids.

claim: The pausing profile at promoters with TFIID-dependent core promoter elements is highly dependent on the promoter sequence.
source: This indicates that lifting a promoter with TFIID-dependent core promoter elements out of its genomic chromatin context does not abolish Pol II pausing and confirms that the pausing profile at those promoters is highly dependent on the promoter sequence.
evidence: This is confirmed by the experimental data showing similar Pol II profiles on plasmids and at endogenous loci.

claim: Pol II pausing can be recapitulated on the plasmid for RpL13A when a larger 2 kb region surrounding the core promoter was cloned into the plasmid, but not with a smaller 300 bp region.
source: We found that Pol II pausing can be recapitulated on the plasmid for RpL13A when a larger 2 kb region surrounding the core promoter was cloned into the plasmid, but not with a smaller 300 bp region (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The plasmid with the larger 2 kb region of RpL13A showed high levels of H3K4me3, similar to the endogenous Rpl13A promoter.
source: The plasmid with the larger region showed high levels of H3K4me3, similar to the endogenous Rpl13A promoter, while the construct with the smaller insertion did not (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ChIP-seq data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Paused Pol II is lost after treatment with triptolide on the plasmid.
source: The results show that paused Pol II is indeed lost after treatment with triptolide and that the degree of loss is proportional to the stability of Pol II on the endogenous promoter.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2B.

claim: The degree of loss of paused Pol II after triptolide treatment on the plasmid is proportional to the stability of Pol II on the endogenous promoter.
source: The results show that paused Pol II is indeed lost after treatment with triptolide and that the degree of loss is proportional to the stability of Pol II on the endogenous promoter.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing triptolide treatment effects on plasmids and endogenous loci in Figure 2B.

claim: The promoter-specific stability of paused Pol II can be measured on a plasmid.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Pol II not only pauses on the plasmid, but that the promoter-specific stability of paused Pol II can, to some extent, be measured on a plasmid.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data showing triptolide effects on plasmids.

claim: Strong Pol II pausing correlates with the presence of downstream elements such as the PB, MTE and DPE.
source: Strong Pol II pausing correlates with the presence of downstream elements such as the PB, MTE and DPE (Chen et al., 2013; Gaertner et al., 2012; Gilchrist et al., 2010; Hendrix et al., 2008; Kwak et al., 2013; Shao and Zeitlinger, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Changing the position of the DPE relative to the Inr alters Pol II pausing.
source: These sequences may be directly implicated in Pol II pausing since they are located near the site of paused Pol II, and changing the position of the DPE relative to the Inr alters Pol II pausing (Kwak et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Replacing the entire downstream promoter sequence with that of a stably paused promoter increased the stability of Pol II pausing.
source: While it was difficult to judge whether the wildtype and hybrid promoters had a different Pol II profile under control conditions, we found that a higher fraction of paused Pol II was reproducibly maintained on the hybrid promoters after triptolide treatment compared to the wild-type promoter (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Downstream promoter sequences influence the stability of Pol II pausing.
source: Taken together, these results confirm that downstream promoter sequences indeed influence the stability of Pol II pausing and we will now refer to MTE, DPE and PB collectively as pausing elements.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data on downstream sequence swapping.

claim: The TATA box is often enriched among promoters with the lowest amount of Pol II pausing.
source: The TATA box is often enriched among promoters with the lowest amount of Pol II pausing (Chen et al., 2013; Day et al., 2016; Gaertner et al., 2012; Shao and Zeitlinger, 2017), and there is evidence in mammalian cells that it promotes the release of paused Pol II (Amir-Zilberstein et al., 2007; Montanuy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: There is evidence in mammalian cells that the TATA box promotes the release of paused Pol II.
source: The TATA box is often enriched among promoters with the lowest amount of Pol II pausing (Chen et al., 2013; Day et al., 2016; Gaertner et al., 2012; Shao and Zeitlinger, 2017), and there is evidence in mammalian cells that it promotes the release of paused Pol II (Amir-Zilberstein et al., 2007; Montanuy et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some promoters, including the hsp70 promoter, contain a TATA box and yet show a strong pausing profile.
source: However, some promoters, including the hsp70 promoter, contain a TATA box and yet show a strong pausing profile (Buckley et al., 2014; Gilchrist et al., 2010; Kwak et al., 2013), questioning the simple model of TATA promoting pause release.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Promoters with a pausing element or an Inr tended to have a long Pol II half-life (median ~25 min).
source: As expected, promoters with a pausing element or an Inr tended to have a long Pol II half-life (median ~25 min) and promoters with both elements displayed an even longer half-life (median ~30 min), consistent with them functioning together (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: Promoters with both a pausing element and an Inr displayed an even longer Pol II half-life (median ~30 min).
source: As expected, promoters with a pausing element or an Inr tended to have a long Pol II half-life (median ~25 min) and promoters with both elements displayed an even longer half-life (median ~30 min), consistent with them functioning together (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: Any combination of core promoter elements that contained a predicted TATA box showed a shorter median half-life of paused Pol II (medians 15–19 min).
source: Also consistent with previous findings (Chen et al., 2013; Day et al., 2016; Shao and Zeitlinger, 2017), any combination that contained a predicted TATA box showed a shorter median half-life of paused Pol II (medians 15–19 min).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: The median half-life of promoters with a pausing element decreased from ~25 min to ~15 min in the presence of TATA.
source: For example, the median half-life of promoters with a pausing element decreased from ~25 min to ~15 min in the presence of TATA (Wilcoxon p<10−4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis in Figure 4A.

claim: Replacing the entire upstream sequence of the TATA-less promoters pk, comm2 and dve with that of the TATA-containing promoter Act5C reduced Pol II pausing in all constructs as compared to the wild-type promoter.
source: When we then analyzed the stability of Pol II pausing after triptolide treatment (1 hr for pk and dve, 40 min for comm2), we observed reduced Pol II in all constructs as compared to the wild-type promoter (Figure 4C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The effect of replacing the upstream sequence with a TATA-containing region was relatively small for the comm2 and dve promoter and only the pk promoter showed a strong, almost two-fold, reduction in paused Pol II.
source: However, the effect was relatively small for the comm2 and dve promoter and only the pk promoter showed a strong, almost two-fold, reduction in paused Pol II.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4D.

claim: Inserting a canonical TATA-box sequence (TATAAAA) in the pk promoter reduced the stability of Pol II pausing, albeit to a lesser extent than when the entire upstream region was replaced.
source: We found that in the pk promoter (but not the comm2 and dve promoter), this small change indeed reduced the stability of Pol II pausing, albeit to a lesser extent than when the entire upstream region was replaced (Figure 4C and D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The TATA box may play a role in destabilizing paused Pol II, but the overall promoter context plays an important role.
source: This suggests that the TATA box may indeed play a role in destabilizing paused Pol II, but that the overall promoter context plays an important role, too.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing variable effects of TATA insertion.

claim: The Inr functions synergistically with the TATA box in transcription if the two elements are optimally spaced from each other.
source: The Inr functions synergistically with the TATA box in transcription if the two elements are optimally spaced from each other (Emami et al., 1997; Malecová et al., 2007; O'Shea-Greenfield and Smale, 1992; Xu et al., 2011), but on the other hand, the Inr is overall more highly enriched among highly paused genes (Gilchrist et al., 2010; Hendrix et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The Inr is overall more highly enriched among highly paused genes.
source: The Inr functions synergistically with the TATA box in transcription if the two elements are optimally spaced from each other (Emami et al., 1997; Malecová et al., 2007; O'Shea-Greenfield and Smale, 1992; Xu et al., 2011), but on the other hand, the Inr is overall more highly enriched among highly paused genes (Gilchrist et al., 2010; Hendrix et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Replacing both the upstream region and the Inr of the dve promoter with sequences from the TATA-containing Act5C promoter resulted in a strong, more than three-fold reduction in the stability of Pol II pausing.
source: Indeed, this replacement resulted in a strong, more than three-fold reduction in the stability of Pol II pausing (Figure 5B and C), suggesting that the type of Inr made a critical difference in this promoter context.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5B and C.

claim: Replacing only the Inr of the dve promoter with that from Act5C resulted in a strong reduction in Pol II pausing stability.
source: However, even when we only replaced the Inr and not the upstream region in the dve promoter, we also observed a strong reduction in Pol II pausing stability (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 5B and C.

claim: The Inr sequence itself is an important determinant of Pol II pausing, even independently of the upstream TATA box.
source: These results suggest that the Inr sequence itself is an important determinant of Pol II pausing, even independently of the upstream TATA box.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data on Inr replacement.

claim: The Inr sequence surrounding the first transcribed base of stably paused promoters is best described by the motif TYAGTY.
source: The Inr sequence surrounding the first transcribed base of stably paused promoters is best described by the motif TYAGTY (Figure 6B left).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: Inr sequences of TATA-containing promoters are more degenerate with frequent mismatches to the Inr consensus sequences.
source: In contrast, Inr sequences of TATA-containing promoters are more degenerate with frequent mismatches to the Inr consensus sequences (Figure 6B right).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: The most striking difference between stably paused promoters and TATA-containing promoters is that the consensus Inr of stably paused promoters contains a G at the +2 position.
source: However, the most striking difference is that the consensus Inr of stably paused promoters contains a G at the next position (the +2). Stably paused promoters contain a G in 90% of cases, while TATA-containing promoters have a G at this position in only 26% (p<10−46).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: Stably paused promoters contain a G at the +2 position in 90% of cases.
source: However, the most striking difference is that the consensus Inr of stably paused promoters contains a G at the next position (the +2). Stably paused promoters contain a G in 90% of cases, while TATA-containing promoters have a G at this position in only 26% (p<10−46).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis.

claim: TATA-containing promoters have a G at the +2 position in only 26% of cases.
source: However, the most striking difference is that the consensus Inr of stably paused promoters contains a G at the next position (the +2). Stably paused promoters contain a G in 90% of cases, while TATA-containing promoters have a G at this position in only 26% (p<10−46).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis.

claim: Promoters with an Inr-G variant had a median Pol II half-life of ~44 min.
source: Promoters with an Inr-G variant had a median Pol II half-life of ~44 min, compared to ~14 min for promoters with the Inr-nonG variant (Wilcoxon p<10−48) or ~18 min for promoters with a pausing element (Wilcoxon p<10−24).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: Promoters with the Inr-nonG variant had a median Pol II half-life of ~14 min.
source: Promoters with an Inr-G variant had a median Pol II half-life of ~44 min, compared to ~14 min for promoters with the Inr-nonG variant (Wilcoxon p<10−48) or ~18 min for promoters with a pausing element (Wilcoxon p<10−24).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: When the Inr-G variant was found in combination with a pausing element, the median Pol II half-life was almost 60 min.
source: When the Inr-G variant was found in combination with a pausing element, the median Pol II half-life was almost 60 min (compared to ~14 min for the Inr-nonG variant, Wilcoxon p<10−62).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: While the pausing elements contribute to Pol II pausing, they strongly depend on the Inr-G variant, which overall has the strongest effect on Pol II pausing.
source: This suggests that while the pausing elements contribute to Pol II pausing, they strongly depend on the Inr-G variant, which overall has the strongest effect on Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is inferred from the genome-wide analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: The presence of TATA was still correlated with shorter Pol II half-lives (median ~13 min).
source: Interestingly, the presence of TATA was still correlated with shorter Pol II half-lives (median ~13 min), but the variant of Inr that was present made a strong difference (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: Promoters with a combination of TATA and Inr-nonG had slightly shorter half-lives (median ~11 min).
source: While promoters with a combination of TATA and Inr-nonG had slightly shorter half-lives (median ~11 min), TATA in combination with the Inr-G variant showed very stable Pol II pausing (median ~59 min, Wilcoxon p<10−7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: TATA in combination with the Inr-G variant showed very stable Pol II pausing (median ~59 min).
source: While promoters with a combination of TATA and Inr-nonG had slightly shorter half-lives (median ~11 min), TATA in combination with the Inr-G variant showed very stable Pol II pausing (median ~59 min, Wilcoxon p<10−7).
evidence: This is demonstrated by genome-wide analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: The Inr acts dominantly over TATA in its effect on Pol II pausing.
source: This suggests that the Inr acts dominantly over TATA in its effect on Pol II pausing, which explains our earlier observations that introducing a TATA upstream region alone only had a small effect on stably paused promoters.
evidence: This is inferred from the genome-wide analysis and experimental data.

claim: Mutating the G at the +2 position of the Inr to A or T at the dve promoter resulted in a dramatic reduction in the stability of paused Pol II.
source: Strikingly, we observed a dramatic reduction in the stability of paused Pol II in the mutated constructs relative to the wild-type construct (Figure 7C and D). The dve promoter showed an almost five-fold decrease when mutated to either T or A.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 7C and D.

claim: The pk and SCP promoters showed a ~ 2 fold reduction in Pol II pausing stability when the G at +2 was mutated.
source: Even the pk and SCP promoters, which have more downstream pausing elements (Table S1) showed a ~ 2 fold reduction.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 7D.

claim: The G in the Inr is critical for stable Pol II pausing in Drosophila.
source: These results show that the G in the Inr is indeed critical for stable Pol II pausing in Drosophila.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis experiments.

claim: Reporter ChIP-nexus can be used to analyze the role of promoter sequences in Pol II pausing and uncover previously unknown roles of promoter elements.
source: More generally, this discovery demonstrates that reporter ChIP-nexus can be used to analyze the role of promoter sequences in Pol II pausing and uncover previously unknown roles of promoter elements.
evidence: This is concluded from the successful application of the method.

claim: Pol II pausing is remarkably well recapitulated on a plasmid.
source: Here, we found that Pol II pausing is remarkably well recapitulated on a plasmid and that its stability can be measured on the plasmid by treatment with triptolide.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data throughout the Results section.

claim: Replacement of core promoter regions bound by TFIID tended to change the stability of paused Pol II in the expected direction.
source: We found that replacement of core promoter regions bound by TFIID tended to change the stability of paused Pol II in the expected direction, but the overall sequence context of the promoter was still important.
evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data on promoter swapping.

claim: The Inr sequence played a strong role in the stability of Pol II pausing.
source: Most notably, we found that the Inr sequence played a strong role in the stability of Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: Promoters with stable Pol II pausing are highly enriched for Inr sequences resembling the consensus TYAGTY.
source: Promoters with stable Pol II pausing are highly enriched for Inr sequences resembling the consensus TYAGTY, which closely matches the Inr derived from functional studies (TCAKTY) (Hultmark et al., 1986; Purnell et al., 1994) and from computational analyses (TCAGTY and TCAGTT) (FitzGerald et al., 2006; Ohler et al., 2002; Stark et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis in Figure 6B and supported by citations.

claim: A strong consensus Inr sequence promotes Pol II pausing.
source: This in turn suggests that a strong consensus Inr sequence promotes Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence analysis and experimental data.

claim: Promoters with a TATA box tend to have more degenerate Inr sequences.
source: Promoters with a TATA box, in contrast, tend to have more degenerate Inr sequences.
evidence: This is demonstrated by sequence analysis in Figure 6B.

claim: The TATA box and Inr co-occur relatively infrequently in both Drosophila and human promoters.
source: This explains why previous genomic sequence analyses have found these two elements to co-occur relatively infrequently in both Drosophila and human promoters (Chen et al., 2013; FitzGerald et al., 2006; Jin et al., 2006; Ohler et al., 2002; Vo Ngoc et al., 2017a), although biochemical experiments clearly show that they function synergistically in transcription (Emami et al., 1997; Malecová et al., 2007; O'Shea-Greenfield and Smale, 1992; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: G and T at the +2 position of the Inr are equally functional in transcription assays in vitro.
source: Although G and T at this position are equally functional in transcription assays in vitro (Lo and Smale, 1996), stably paused promoters predominantly contain the Inr-G variant.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mutating the G at +2 to an A or T drastically reduced Pol II pausing in the reporter assay.
source: Mutating this G to an A or T drastically reduced Pol II pausing in our assay, suggesting that the G is indeed important for stable Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: The degenerate Inr-nonG sequences in TATA-containing promoters may represent a tradeoff between influencing start site selection and promoting TATA-dependent transcription while being weakened in their ability to stabilize Pol II pausing.
source: It is therefore possible that the degenerate Inr-nonG sequences in TATA-containing promoters represent a tradeoff. On one hand, these Inr sequences probably have sufficient sequence information to influence start site selection and promote TATA-dependent transcription. On the other hand, they may be weakened in their ability to stabilize Pol II pausing and thereby allow a mode of transcription with reduced Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is speculated based on the experimental and sequence analysis data.

claim: An Inr-G variant (TCAGTT) was identified in comparative Drosophila genomics analyses as the most conserved Inr sequence.
source: Interestingly, an Inr-G variant (TCAGTT) was identified in comparative Drosophila genomics analyses as the most conserved Inr sequence (Stark et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The G variant of the Inr may be under evolutionarily selection in paused promoters.
source: This suggests that the G variant may be under evolutionarily selection in paused promoters, consistent with Pol II pausing playing a critical role in keeping the promoter open (Gilchrist et al., 2008) and achieving coordinated gene expression during development (Lagha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation data and supported by citations.

claim: Human Inr sequences are often more degenerate and do not show a significant enrichment of G at the +2.
source: It is important to point out that while the G is conserved in Drosophila, human Inr sequences are often more degenerate and do not show a significant enrichment of G at the +2 (Carninci et al., 2006; Frith et al., 2008; Lo and Smale, 1996; Vo Ngoc et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is possible that human Inr variants also differentially affect Pol II pausing.
source: It is therefore possible that human Inr variants also differentially affect Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings in Drosophila.

claim: TFIID is a large, flexible multi-subunit complex that can simultaneously bind to the TATA box, the Inr, and the pausing elements.
source: TFIID is a large, flexible multi-subunit complex that can simultaneously bind to the TATA box, the Inr, and the pausing elements (Louder et al., 2016; Patel et al., 2018), thereby promoting the assembly of the transcription initiation complex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: There is accumulating evidence that TFIID promotes Pol II re-initiation.
source: For example, there is accumulating evidence that TFIID promotes Pol II re-initiation (Joo et al., 2017; Oelgeschläger et al., 1998; Yudkovsky et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Genome-wide ChIP-nexus data show that TFIID binding extends beyond the pausing position in vivo.
source: Furthermore, genome-wide ChIP-nexus data show that TFIID binding extends beyond the pausing position in vivo (Shao and Zeitlinger, 2017), raising the intriguing possibility that TFIID plays a role in the coordination between consecutive rounds of Pol II initiation, pausing, and pause release.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: If TFIID remains bound after initiation, it is possible that it influences the stability of Pol II pausing in a promoter-specific fashion.
source: If TFIID remains bound after initiation, it is possible that it influences the stability of Pol II pausing in a promoter-specific fashion.
evidence: This is speculated based on the TFIID binding data.

claim: If TFIID binds tightly to the Inr and downstream promoter elements, Pol II may initiate and traverse the early transcribed region more slowly, and hence may be more likely to become stably paused.
source: If TFIID binds tightly to the Inr and downstream promoter elements, Pol II may initiate and traverse the early transcribed region more slowly, and hence may be more likely to become stably paused (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: If TFIID is more tightly bound to the promoter upstream through the TATA box, then Pol II initiation and early transcription may occur in a less constrained fashion, which may promote pause release.
source: In contrast, if TFIID is more tightly bound to the promoter upstream through the TATA box, then Pol II initiation and early transcription may occur in a less constrained fashion, which may promote pause release (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Tight DNA contacts of TFIID in the presence of the TATA box is supported by biochemical experiments and single-molecule footprinting studies.
source: These tight DNA contacts in the presence of the TATA box is supported by biochemical experiments (Lee et al., 1991; Starr and Hawley, 1991), as well as more recent single-molecule footprinting studies (Krebs et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reporter-ChIP-nexus is a useful method for studying the relationship between promoter sequence and Pol II pausing.
source: We found that reporter-ChIP-nexus is a useful method for studying the relationship between promoter sequence and Pol II pausing.
evidence: This is concluded from the successful application of the method throughout the study.

claim: Reporter-ChIP-nexus recapitulates the endogenous Pol II dynamics at the promoters tested.
source: This plasmid-based assay recapitulates the endogenous Pol II dynamics at the promoters tested and has sufficient sensitivity to identify changes in Pol II pausing upon promoter sequence alterations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data comparing plasmid and endogenous profiles.

claim: Reporter-ChIP-nexus has sufficient sensitivity to identify changes in Pol II pausing upon promoter sequence alterations.
source: This plasmid-based assay recapitulates the endogenous Pol II dynamics at the promoters tested and has sufficient sensitivity to identify changes in Pol II pausing upon promoter sequence alterations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the mutagenesis experiments throughout the study.

claim: The accuracy and reproducibility of the reporter-ChIP-nexus assay is higher for promoters with longer Pol II half-lives.
source: Currently, the accuracy and reproducibility of the assay is higher for promoters with longer Pol II half-lives since longer triptolide treatment times reduce experimental fluctuations in handling and drug penetration.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experience with the assay.

claim: Reporter-ChIP-nexus promises to open new possibilities for measuring the stability of Pol II pausing at individual promoter sequences in the future.
source: Taken together, reporter-ChIP-nexus promises to open new possibilities for measuring the stability of Pol II pausing at individual promoter sequences in the future.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement based on the demonstrated utility of the method.
